Main.sentence: Cannabis ( /ˈkænəbɪs/ ),  commonly known as marijuana ( /ˌmærəˈwɑːnə/ ),  weed , pot , and ganja , ___E:among other names U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_slang_names_for_cannabis)___ , is a non-chemically uniform ___E:psychoactive drug U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoactive_drug)___ from the Cannabis plant.

Native to Central or South Asia, cannabis has been used as a drug for both recreational and ___E:entheogenic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entheogenic_use_of_cannabis)___ purposes and in various ___E:traditional medicines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_medicine)___ for centuries. ___E:Tetrahydrocannabinol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydrocannabinol)___ (THC) is the main psychoactive component of cannabis, which is one of the 483 known compounds in the plant, including at least 65 other ___E:cannabinoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid)___ , such as ___E:cannabidiol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabidiol)___ (CBD).

Cannabis can be used ___E:by smoking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_smoking)___ , ___E:vaporizing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporizer_(inhalation_device))___ , ___E:within food U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_edible)___ , or ___E:as an extract U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tincture_of_cannabis)___ .

Cannabis has ___E:various mental and physical effects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_cannabis)___ , which include ___E:euphoria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoria)___ , ___E:altered states of mind U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_states_of_mind)___ and ___E:sense of time U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_and_time_perception)___ , difficulty concentrating, ___E:impaired short-term memory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_and_memory)___ , impaired ___E:body movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_skill)___ (balance and fine psychomotor control), relaxation, and an increase in ___E:appetite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appetite)___ .
Onset of effects is felt within minutes when smoked, but may take up to 90 minutes when eaten (as orally consumed drugs must be digested and absorbed).

The effects last for two to six hours, depending on the amount used. At high doses, mental effects can include ___E:anxiety U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiety)___ , delusions (including ___E:ideas of reference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideas_of_reference)___ ), ___E:hallucinations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucination)___ , ___E:panic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_attack)___ , ___E:paranoia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranoia)___ , and ___E:psychosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_and_psychosis)___ .
There is a strong relation between cannabis use and the risk of psychosis, though the direction of ___E:causality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causality)___ is debated.

Physical effects include increased heart rate, difficulty breathing, nausea, and behavioral problems in children whose mothers used cannabis during pregnancy; short-term side effects may also include ___E:dry mouth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerostomia)___ and red eyes. ___E:Long-term adverse effects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-term_effects_of_cannabis)___ may include addiction, decreased ___E:mental ability U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurocognition)___ in those who started regular use as adolescents,  heart disease, chronic coughing, susceptibility to ___E:respiratory infections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_tract_infection)___ , and ___E:cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid_hyperemesis_syndrome)___ .
Cannabis is mostly used recreationally or as a medicinal drug, although it may also be used for spiritual purposes.
There is mixed and inconclusive evidence on the benefits of ___E:medical cannabis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_cannabis)___ .
In 2013, between 128 and 232 million people used cannabis (2.7% to 4.9% of the global population between the ages of 15 and 65).

It is the most commonly used largely-illegal drug in the world, with the highest use among ___E:adults in Zambia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Zambia)___ , the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_the_United_States)___ , ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Canada)___ , and ___E:Nigeria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Nigeria)___ .
Since the 1970s, the potency of illicit cannabis has increased, with THC levels rising and CBD levels dropping.

Cannabis plants have been grown since at least the 3rd millennium BCE and there is evidence of it being smoked for its psychoactive effects around 500 BCE in the ___E:Pamir Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamir_Mountains)___ , Central Asia. Since the 14th century, cannabis has been subject to legal restrictions.
The possession, use, and cultivation of cannabis has been ___E:illegal in most countries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_cannabis)___ since the 20th century.

In 2013, ___E:Uruguay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Uruguay)___ became the first country to ___E:legalize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_legalization)___ recreational use of cannabis.

Other countries to do so are Canada, ___E:Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Georgia_(country))___ , ___E:Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Germany)___ , ___E:Luxembourg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Luxembourg)___ , ___E:Malta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Malta)___ , ___E:South Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_South_Africa)___ , and ___E:Thailand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Thailand)___ .

In the U.S., the recreational use of cannabis is legalized in ___E:24 states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_cannabis_by_U.S._jurisdiction)___ , 3 territories, and the ___E:District of Columbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Washington,_D.C.)___ , though the drug remains ___E:federally illegal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Schedule_I_drugs_(US))___ .

In ___E:Australia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Australia)___ , it is legalized only in the ___E:Australian Capital Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory)___ .

The origins of Cannabis are linked to a ___E:Scythian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythian)___ word.    The ___E:ancient Greeks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greeks)___ may have learned of the use of cannabis, which they called κάνναβις , by observing Scythian funerals, during which cannabis was consumed.
In ___E:Akkadian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_language)___ , cannabis was known as qunubu ( 𐎯𐎫𐎠𐎭𐏂 ).
The word was adopted in to the ___E:Hebrew U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language)___ as qaneh bosem ( קָנֶה בֹּשׂם ).

The Latin term cannabis derived from Greek evolved into Proto-Germanic * xan(a)paz , yielding various Germanic forms (Old Norse hampr , Old English hænep , Old Saxon hanup , Old High German hanaf ) and ultimately modern British English "hemp."
Medical cannabis, or medical marijuana, refers to the use of herbal cannabis or its preparations to treat disease or improve symptoms.

There is no single agreed-upon definition (e.g., ___E:cannabinoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoids)___ derived from cannabis and ___E:synthetic cannabinoid analogs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_cannabinoids)___ are also used).
The rigorous scientific study of cannabis as a medicine has been hampered by production restrictions and by the fact that it is classified as an illegal drug by many governments.
Overall, there is mixed evidence on the benefits of cannabis-based medicines, frequent mild adverse effects, and generally low-to-moderate quality of evidence.

There is some evidence suggesting cannabis can be used to ___E:reduce nausea and vomiting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiemetic)___ during ___E:chemotherapy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotherapy)___ , to improve appetite in people with ___E:HIV/AIDS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS)___ , or to treat ___E:chronic pain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronic_pain)___ and ___E:muscle spasms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_spasms)___ .
Evidence for its use for other medical applications is insufficient for drawing conclusions about safety or efficacy.
There is evidence supporting the use of cannabis or its derivatives in the treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, neuropathic pain, and multiple sclerosis.
Lower levels of evidence support its use for AIDS ___E:wasting syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachexia)___ , epilepsy, rheumatoid arthritis, and glaucoma.

The medical use of cannabis is legal only in a limited number of territories, including Canada,  ___E:Belgium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium)___ , Australia, the ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands)___ , New Zealand,   Spain, and ___E:many U.S. states U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_cannabis_in_the_United_States)___ .
This usage generally requires a prescription, and distribution is usually done within a framework defined by local laws.
Being under the effects of cannabis is usually referred to as being "high".
Cannabis consumption has both psychoactive and physiological effects.

The "high" experience can vary widely, based (among other things) on the user's prior experience with cannabis, and the type of cannabis consumed.  : p647 When smoking cannabis, a ___E:euphoriant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoria)___ effect can occur within minutes of smoking.  : p104 Aside from a subjective change in perception and mood, the most common short-term physical and neurological effects include increased heart rate, increased appetite, impairment of short-term and working memory, and impairment of ___E:psychomotor coordination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychomotor_coordination)___ .

Additional desired effects from consuming cannabis include relaxation, a general ___E:alteration of conscious perception U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_state_of_consciousness)___ , increased awareness of sensation, increased ___E:libido U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libido)___  and ___E:distortions in the perception of time U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_and_time_perception)___ and space.

In some cases, cannabis can lead to ___E:dissociative U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissociation_(psychology))___ states such as ___E:depersonalization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depersonalization)___   and ___E:derealization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derealization)___ .

Cannabis has held sacred status in several religions and has served as an ___E:entheogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entheogen)___ – a ___E:chemical substance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_substance)___ used in religious, ___E:shamanic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamanism)___ , or ___E:spiritual U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirituality)___ contexts  – in the Indian subcontinent since the ___E:Vedic period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period)___ .

The earliest known reports regarding the sacred status of cannabis in the Indian subcontinent come from the ___E:Atharva Veda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atharva_Veda)___ , estimated to have been composed sometime around 1400 BCE.  The Hindu god ___E:Shiva U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva)___ is described as a cannabis user, known as the "Lord of ___E:bhang U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhang)___ ".  : p19

In modern culture, the spiritual use of cannabis has been spread by the disciples of the ___E:Rastafari movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rastafari_movement)___ who use cannabis as a ___E:sacrament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrament)___ and as an aid to meditation.

Many different ways to consume cannabis involve heat to ___E:decarboxylate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decarboxylation)___ ___E:THCA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydrocannabinolic_acid)___ into THC;   common modes include:
In 2013, between 128 and 232 million people used cannabis (2.7% to 4.9% of the global population between the ages of 15 and 65).

Cannabis is by far the most widely used illicit substance,  with the highest use among adults (as of 2018 [update] ) in ___E:Zambia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Zambia)___ , the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_the_United_States)___ , ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Canada)___ , and ___E:Nigeria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Nigeria)___ .
Between 1973 and 1978, eleven states decriminalized marijuana.

In 2001, ___E:Nevada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Nevada)___ reduced marijuana possession to a misdemeanor and since 2012, several other states have decriminalized and even legalized marijuana.
In 2018, surveys indicated that almost half of the people in the United States had tried marijuana, 16% had used it in the past year, and 11% had used it in the past month.

In 2014, surveys said daily marijuana use amongst US college students had reached its highest level since records began in 1980, rising from 3.5% in 2007 to 5.9% in 2014 and had surpassed daily cigarette use.

In the US, men are over twice as likely to use marijuana as women, and 18–29-year-olds are six times more likely to use as over-65-year-olds.  In 2015, a record 44% of the US population has tried marijuana in their lifetime, an increase from 38% in 2013 and 33% in 1985.
Marijuana use in the United States is three times above the global average, but in line with other Western democracies.

Forty-four percent of American 12th graders have tried the drug at least once, and the typical age of first-use is 16, similar to the typical age of first-use for alcohol but lower than the first-use age for other illicit drugs.
A 2022 ___E:Gallup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup,_Inc.)___ poll concluded Americans are smoking more marijuana than cigarettes for the first time.
Acute negative effects may include anxiety and panic, impaired attention and memory, an increased risk of psychotic symptoms, [b] the inability to think clearly, and an increased risk of accidents.

Cannabis impairs a person's driving ability, and ___E:THC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydrocannabinol)___ was the illicit drug most frequently found in the blood of drivers who have been involved in ___E:vehicle crashes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_collision)___ .
Those with THC in their system are from three to seven times more likely to be the cause of vehicle crash than those who had not used either cannabis or alcohol.   [c]
Some immediate undesired side effects include a decrease in short-term memory, dry mouth, impaired motor skills, reddening of the eyes,  dizziness, feeling tired and vomiting.

Some users may experience an episode of acute ___E:psychosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis)___ , which usually abates after six hours, but in rare instances, heavy users may find the symptoms continuing for many days.
Legalization has increased the rates at which children are exposed to cannabis, particularly from edibles.
While the toxicity and lethality of THC in children is not known, they are at risk for encephalopathy, hypotension, respiratory depression severe enough to require ventilation, somnolence and coma.
A systematic meta analysis showed that cannabis users double the chance of dying from heart disease.
Cannabis users had a 29% higher risk of heart attack and a 20% higher risk of stroke than non-users.
There is an association between cannabis use and suicide, particularly in younger users.
A 16-month survey of Oregon and Alaska emergency departments found a report of the death of an adult who had been admitted for acute cannabis toxicity.

A recent study in 2025 suggests that individuals diagnosed with cannabis use disorder—characterized by an inability to stop using cannabis despite its negative effects—face a nearly threefold increase in ___E:mortality rates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortality_rate)___ compared to those without the condition over a five-year period.
The research indicates that people with this disorder are ten times more likely to die by suicide than the general population.
Additionally, they have a higher risk of death from trauma, drug poisoning, and lung cancer.

In a separate study researchers found an increase in ___E:schizophrenia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia)___ and ___E:psychosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis)___ cases in ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)___ linked to cannabis use disorder following the drug's legalization.

A 2015 meta-analysis found that, although a longer period of abstinence was associated with smaller magnitudes of impairment, both retrospective and ___E:prospective U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospective_memory)___ memory were impaired in cannabis users.
The authors concluded that some, but not all, of the deficits associated with cannabis use were reversible.

A 2012 meta-analysis found that deficits in most domains of cognition persisted beyond the acute period of intoxication, but was not evident in studies where subjects were abstinent for more than 25 days.  Few high quality studies have been performed on the long-term effects of cannabis on cognition, and the results were generally inconsistent.
Furthermore, ___E:effect sizes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_size)___ of significant findings were generally small.

One review concluded that, although most cognitive faculties were unimpaired by cannabis use, residual deficits occurred in ___E:executive functions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_function)___ .

Impairments in executive functioning are most consistently found in older populations, which may reflect heavier cannabis exposure, or developmental effects associated with adolescent cannabis use.  One review found three prospective cohort studies that examined the relationship between self-reported cannabis use and ___E:intelligence quotient U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_quotient)___ (IQ).

The study following the largest number of heavy cannabis users reported that IQ declined between ages 7–13 and age 38. Poorer school performance and increased incidence of leaving school early were both associated with cannabis use, although a causal relationship was not established.
Cannabis users demonstrated increased activity in task-related brain regions, consistent with reduced processing efficiency.

A reduced ___E:quality of life U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_of_life)___ is associated with heavy cannabis use, although the relationship is inconsistent and weaker than for tobacco and other substances.
The direction of ___E:cause and effect U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cause_and_effect)___ , however, is unclear.
The ___E:long-term effects of cannabis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-term_effects_of_cannabis)___ are not clear.

There are concerns surrounding ___E:memory and cognition problems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_and_memory)___ , risk of addiction, and the risk of ___E:schizophrenia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia)___ in young people.

Although global abnormalities in ___E:white matter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_matter)___ and ___E:grey matter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey_matter)___ are not consistently associated with cannabis use,  reduced ___E:hippocampal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocampus)___ volume is consistently found.  ___E:Amygdala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amygdala)___ abnormalities are sometimes reported, although findings are inconsistent.

Cannabis use is associated with increased recruitment of task-related areas, such as the ___E:dorsolateral prefrontal cortex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorsolateral_prefrontal_cortex)___ , which is thought to reflect compensatory activity due to reduced processing efficiency.
Cannabis use is also associated with downregulation of ___E:CB1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid_receptor_type_1)___ receptors.
The magnitude of down regulation is associated with cumulative cannabis exposure, and is reversed after one month of abstinence.
There is limited evidence that chronic cannabis use can reduce levels of ___E:glutamate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamate)___ metabolites in the human brain.

About 9% of those who experiment with marijuana eventually become dependent according to ___E:DSM-IV (1994) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnostic_and_Statistical_Manual_of_Mental_Disorders)___ criteria.
A 2013 review estimates daily use is associated with a 10–20% rate of dependence.

The highest risk of cannabis dependence is found in those with a history of poor academic achievement, ___E:deviant behavior U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deviance_(sociology))___ in childhood and adolescence, rebelliousness, poor parental relationships, or a parental history of drug and alcohol problems.
Of daily users, about 50% experience withdrawal upon cessation of use (i.e. are dependent), characterized by sleep problems, irritability, dysphoria, and craving.
Cannabis withdrawal is less severe than withdrawal from alcohol.

According to ___E:DSM-5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSM-5)___ criteria, 9% of those who are exposed to cannabis develop cannabis use disorder, compared to 20% for ___E:cocaine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine)___ , 23% for ___E:alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(drug))___ and 68% for ___E:nicotine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotine)___ .
Cannabis use disorder in the DSM-5 involves a combination of DSM-IV criteria for cannabis abuse and dependence, plus the addition of craving, without the criterion related to legal troubles.

From a clinical perspective, two significant school of thought exists for psychiatric conditions associated with cannabis (or cannabinoids) use: transient, non-persistent psychotic reactions, and longer-lasting, persistent disorders that resemble schizophrenia.
The former is formally known as acute cannabis-associated psychotic symptoms (CAPS).

At an epidemiological level, a ___E:dose–response relationship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dose%E2%80%93response_relationship)___ exists between cannabis use and increased risk of ___E:psychosis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis)___ and earlier onset of psychosis.
Although the epidemiological association is robust, evidence to prove a causal relationship is lacking.
Cannabis may also increase the risk of depression, but insufficient research has been performed to draw a conclusion.
Cannabis use is associated with increased risk of anxiety disorders, although causality has not been established.

A review in 2019 found that research was insufficient to determine the safety and efficacy of using cannabis to treat schizophrenia, psychosis, or other ___E:mental disorders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_disorder)___ .
Another found that cannabis during adolescence was associated with an increased risk of developing depression and suicidal behavior later in life, while finding no effect on anxiety.
Heavy, long-term exposure to marijuana may have physical, mental, behavioral and social health consequences.
It may be "associated with diseases of the liver (particularly with co-existing ___E:hepatitis C U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatitis_C)___ ), lungs, heart, and vasculature".

A 2014 review found that while cannabis use may be less harmful than alcohol use, the recommendation to substitute it for ___E:problematic drinking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholism)___ was premature without further study.

Various surveys conducted between 2015 and 2019 found that many users of cannabis substitute it for ___E:prescription drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prescription_drug)___ (including opioids), alcohol, and tobacco; most of those who used it in place of alcohol or tobacco either reduced or stopped their intake of the latter substances.

___E:Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid_hyperemesis_syndrome)___ (CHS) is a severe condition seen in some chronic cannabis users where they have repeated bouts of uncontrollable vomiting for 24–48 hours.
Four cases of death have been reported as a result of CHS.
A limited number of studies have examined the ___E:effects of cannabis smoking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis-associated_respiratory_disease)___ on the respiratory system.

Chronic heavy marijuana smoking is associated with ___E:respiratory infections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_infections)___ ,  coughing, production of sputum, wheezing, and other symptoms of chronic bronchitis.

The available evidence does not support a causal relationship between cannabis use and ___E:chronic obstructive pulmonary disease U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronic_obstructive_pulmonary_disease)___ .
Short-term use of cannabis is associated with ___E:bronchodilation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronchodilation)___ .

Other side effects of cannabis use include ___E:cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid_hyperemesis_syndrome)___ (CHS), a condition which involves recurrent nausea, cramping abdominal pain, and vomiting.
Cannabis smoke contains thousands of organic and inorganic chemical compounds.

This ___E:tar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tar_(tobacco_residue))___ is chemically similar to that found in tobacco smoke,  and over fifty known ___E:carcinogens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcinogen)___ have been identified in cannabis smoke,  including; nitrosamines, reactive aldehydes, and ___E:polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycyclic_aromatic_hydrocarbon)___ , including benz[a]pyrene.
Cannabis smoke is also inhaled more deeply than tobacco smoke.
As of 2015 [update] , there is no consensus regarding whether cannabis smoking is associated with an increased risk of cancer.
Light and moderate use of cannabis is not believed to increase risk of lung or upper airway cancer.

Evidence for causing these cancers is mixed concerning heavy, long-term use. In general there are far lower risks of pulmonary complications for regular cannabis smokers when compared with those of tobacco.

A 2015 review found an association between cannabis use and the development of testicular ___E:germ cell tumors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_cell_tumor)___ (TGCTs), particularly non- ___E:seminoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminoma)___ TGCTs.
Another 2015 meta-analysis found no association between lifetime cannabis use and risk of head or neck cancer.

Combustion products are not present when using a ___E:vaporizer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporizer_(inhalation_device))___ , consuming THC in pill form, or consuming ___E:cannabis foods U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_foods)___ .
There is concern that cannabis may contribute to cardiovascular disease,  but as of 2018 [update] , evidence of this relationship was unclear.
Research in these events is complicated because cannabis is often used in conjunction with tobacco, and drugs such as alcohol and cocaine that are known to have cardiovascular risk factors.
Smoking cannabis has also been shown to increase the risk of ___E:myocardial infarction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction)___ by 4.8 times for the 60 minutes after consumption.

There is preliminary evidence that cannabis interferes with the ___E:anticoagulant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticoagulant)___ properties of prescription drugs used for ___E:treating blood clots U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrombosis)___ .

As of 2019 [update] , the ___E:mechanisms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanism_of_action)___ for the ___E:anti-inflammatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-inflammatory)___ and possible ___E:pain relieving U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analgesic)___ effects of cannabis were not defined, and there were no governmental regulatory approvals or clinical practices for use of cannabis as a drug.

Emergency room (ER) admissions associated with cannabis use rose significantly from 2012 to 2016; adolescents from age 12–17 had the highest risk.  At one Colorado medical center following legalization, approximately two percent of ER admissions were classified as cannabis users.
The symptoms of one quarter of these users were partially attributed to cannabis (a total of 2567 out of 449,031 patients); other drugs were sometimes involved.

Of these cannabis admissions, one quarter were for ___E:acute psychiatric effects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-term_effects_of_cannabis#Mental_health)___ , primarily ___E:suicidal ideation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicidal_ideation)___ , depression, and anxiety.
An additional third of the cases were for gastrointestinal issues including ___E:cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid_hyperemesis_syndrome)___ .

According to the United States Department of Health and Human Services, there were 455,000 emergency room visits associated with cannabis use in 2011. These statistics include visits in which the patient was treated for a condition induced by or related to recent cannabis use. The drug use must be "implicated" in the emergency department visit, but does not need to be the direct cause of the visit.
Most of the illicit drug emergency room visits involved multiple drugs.
In 129,000 cases, cannabis was the only implicated drug.

A 2022 study found that smoking cannabis using a bong can greatly increase background levels of ___E:fine particulate matter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particulates)___ , a ___E:carcinogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcinogen)___ , in an enclosed space such as a living room. After 15 minutes, mean levels of particulate matter were more than twice the ___E:Environmental Protection Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency)___ hazardous air quality threshold, and after 140 minutes, the concentrations were four times greater than those generated by smoking tobacco using a cigarette or ___E:hookah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hookah)___ .
This suggests secondhand cannabis smoke from bongs may present a health risk to non-smokers.
THC is a weak partial agonist at ___E:CB1 receptors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CB1_receptor)___ , while CBD is a ___E:CB1 receptor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CB1_receptor)___ antagonist.

The CB 1 receptor is found primarily in the brain as well as in some peripheral tissues, and the CB 2 receptor is found primarily in peripheral tissues, but is also expressed in ___E:neuroglial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroglia)___ cells.

THC appears to alter mood and cognition through its agonist actions on the CB 1 receptors, which inhibit a ___E:secondary messenger system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_messenger_system)___ ( ___E:adenylate cyclase U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenylate_cyclase)___ ) in a dose-dependent manner.

Via CB 1 receptor activation, THC indirectly increases ___E:dopamine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopamine)___ release and produces ___E:psychotropic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotropic)___ effects.  ___E:CBD U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabidiol)___ also acts as an ___E:allosteric modulator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allosteric_modulator)___ of the ___E:μ- U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%9C-opioid_receptor)___ and ___E:δ-opioid receptors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%94-opioid_receptor)___ .
THC also potentiates the effects of the ___E:glycine receptors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glycine_receptor)___ .
It is unknown if or how these actions contribute to the effects of cannabis.

The high ___E:lipid-solubility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipophilicity)___ of cannabinoids results in their persisting in the body for long periods of time.  Even after a single administration of THC, detectable levels of THC can be found in the body for weeks or longer (depending on the amount administered and the sensitivity of the assessment method).
Investigators have suggested that this is an important factor in marijuana's effects, perhaps because cannabinoids may accumulate in the body, particularly in the lipid membranes of neurons.

The main psychoactive component of cannabis is ___E:tetrahydrocannabinol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydrocannabinol)___ (THC), which is formed via decarboxylation of ___E:tetrahydrocannabinolic acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahydrocannabinolic_acid)___ (THCA) from the application of heat. Raw leaf is not psychoactive because the ___E:cannabinoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid)___ are in the form of ___E:carboxylic acids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboxylic_acids)___ . [citation needed] THC is one of the 483 known compounds in the plant,  including at least 65 other cannabinoids,  such as ___E:cannabidiol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabidiol)___ (CBD).

THC and its major (inactive) metabolite, ___E:THC-COOH U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THC-COOH)___ , can be measured in blood, urine, hair, oral fluid or sweat using ___E:chromatographic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatographic)___ techniques as part of a drug use testing program or a forensic investigation of a traffic or other criminal offense.

The concentrations obtained from such analyses can often be helpful in distinguishing active use from passive exposure, elapsed time since use, and extent or duration of use. These tests cannot, however, distinguish authorized cannabis smoking for medical purposes from unauthorized recreational smoking.

Commercial cannabinoid ___E:immunoassays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunoassay)___ , often employed as the initial screening method when testing physiological specimens for marijuana presence, have different degrees of cross-reactivity with THC and its metabolites.

Urine contains predominantly THC-COOH, while hair, oral fluid and sweat contain primarily THC.  Blood may contain both substances, with the relative amounts dependent on the recency and extent of usage.

The ___E:Duquenois–Levine test U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duquenois%E2%80%93Levine_test)___ is commonly used as a ___E:screening test U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumptive_and_confirmatory_tests)___ in the field, but it cannot definitively confirm the presence of cannabis, as a large range of substances have been shown to give false positives.
Researchers at John Jay College of Criminal Justice reported that dietary zinc supplements can mask the presence of THC and other drugs in urine.

However, a 2013 study conducted by researchers at the ___E:University of Utah School of Medicine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Utah_School_of_Medicine)___ refute the possibility of self-administered zinc producing false-negative urine drug tests.

CBD is a ___E:5-HT1A receptor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5-HT1A_receptor)___ agonist, which is under laboratory research to determine if it has an ___E:anxiolytic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiolytic)___ effect.
It is often claimed that sativa strains provide a more stimulating psychoactive high while indica strains are more sedating with a body high.  However, this is disputed by researchers.

A 2015 review found that the use of high CBD-to-THC strains of cannabis showed significantly fewer ___E:positive symptoms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_symptoms)___ , such as delusions and hallucinations, better ___E:cognitive function U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_function)___ and both lower risk for developing psychosis, as well as a later age of onset of the illness, compared to cannabis with low CBD-to-THC ratios.

According to the ___E:United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Office_on_Drugs_and_Crime)___ (UNODC), "the amount of THC present in a cannabis sample is generally used as a measure of cannabis potency."  The three main forms of cannabis products are the flower/fruit, resin (hashish), and oil (hash oil).
The UNODC states that cannabis often contains 5% THC content, resin "can contain up to 20% THC content", and that "Cannabis oil may contain more than 60% THC content."
Studies have found that the potency of illicit cannabis has greatly increased since the 1970s, with THC levels rising and CBD levels dropping.
It is unclear, however, whether the increase in THC content has caused people to consume more THC or if users adjust based on the potency of the cannabis.

It is likely that the higher THC content allows people to ingest less tar. At the same time, CBD levels in seized samples have lowered, in part because of the desire to produce higher THC levels and because more illegal growers cultivate indoors using artificial lights.
This helps avoid detection but reduces the CBD production of the plant.

Australia's ___E:National Cannabis Prevention and Information Centre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cannabis_Prevention_and_Information_Centre)___ (NCPIC) states that the buds ( ___E:infructescences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infructescence)___ ) of the female Cannabis plant contain the highest concentration of THC, followed by the leaves.
The stalks and seeds have "much lower THC levels".
The UN states that the leaves can contain ten times less THC than the buds, and the stalks 100 times less THC.

After revisions to ___E:cannabis scheduling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_reclassification_in_the_United_Kingdom)___ in the UK, the government moved cannabis back from a ___E:class C U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_C_drug)___ to a ___E:class B drug U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_B_drug)___ .
A purported reason was the appearance of high potency cannabis.

They believe ___E:skunk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skunk_(cannabis_strain))___ accounts for between 70% and 80% of samples seized by police  (despite the fact that skunk can sometimes be incorrectly mistaken for all types of herbal cannabis).   ___E:Extracts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extract)___ such as ___E:hashish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashish)___ and ___E:hash oil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_oil)___ typically contain more THC than high potency cannabis infructescences.
Hemp buds (or low-potency cannabis buds) laced with ___E:synthetic cannabinoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_cannabinoids)___ started to be sold as cannabis street drug in 2020.

The short-term effects of cannabis can be altered if it has been laced with ___E:opioid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opioid)___ drugs such as heroin or ___E:fentanyl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fentanyl)___ .
The added drugs are meant to enhance the psychoactive properties, add to its weight, and increase profitability, despite the increased danger of overdose.  [d]
Marijuana or marihuana (herbal cannabis)  consists of the dried flowers and fruits and subtending leaves and stems of the female cannabis plant.
This is the most widely consumed form,  containing 3% to 20% THC,  with reports of up to 33% THC.  This is the stock material from which all other preparations are derived.

Although herbal cannabis and ___E:industrial hemp U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemp)___ derive from the same species and contain the psychoactive component (THC), they are distinct strains with unique biochemical compositions and uses. Hemp has lower concentrations of THC and higher concentrations of CBD, which gives lesser psychoactive effects.

Kief is a powder, rich in ___E:trichomes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichome)___ ,  which can be sifted from the leaves, flowers and fruits of ___E:cannabis plants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_sativa)___ and either ___E:consumed in powder form U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_hitter_(smoking))___ or compressed to produce cakes of ___E:hashish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashish)___ .
The word "kif" derives from ___E:colloquial Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colloquial_Arabic)___ كيف kēf/kīf , meaning pleasure .

Hashish (also spelled hasheesh, hashisha, or simply hash) is a concentrated ___E:resin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resin)___ cake or ball produced from pressed kief, the detached trichomes and fine material that falls off cannabis fruits, flowers and leaves,  or from scraping the resin from the surface of the plants and rolling it into balls.
It varies in color from black to golden brown depending upon purity and variety of cultivar it was obtained from.  It can be consumed orally or smoked, and is also vaporized, or 'vaped'.
The term "rosin hash" refers to a high quality solventless product obtained through heat and pressure.

Cannabinoids can be ___E:extracted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraction_(chemistry))___ from cannabis plant matter using high- ___E:proof U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_proof)___ ___E:spirits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbalism#Routes_of_administration)___ (often ___E:grain alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectified_spirit)___ ) to create a ___E:tincture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tincture)___ , often referred to as "green dragon".  : p17 ___E:Nabiximols U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabiximols)___ is a branded product name from a tincture manufacturing pharmaceutical company.

Hash oil is a ___E:resinous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resin)___ matrix of ___E:cannabinoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabinoid)___ obtained from the cannabis plant by ___E:solvent extraction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solvent_extraction)___ ,  formed into a hardened or viscous mass.  Hash oil can be the most potent of the main cannabis products because of its high level of psychoactive compound per its volume, which can vary depending on the plant's mix of essential oils and psychoactive compounds.  ___E:Butane U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butane)___ and ___E:supercritical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercritical_fluid)___ ___E:carbon dioxide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide)___ hash oil have become popular in recent years.

There are many varieties of cannabis infusions owing to the variety of non-volatile solvents used.  The plant material is mixed with the solvent and then pressed and filtered to express the oils of the plant into the solvent.
Examples of solvents used in this process are cocoa butter, dairy butter, cooking oil, ___E:glycerine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glycerine)___ , and skin moisturizers.
Depending on the solvent, these may be used in ___E:cannabis foods U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_foods)___ or applied topically.
Marihuana prensada ('pressed marijuana') is a cannabis-derived product widespread among the lower classes of South America,  especially from the 90s.
Locally it is known as " paraguayo " or " paragua ", since its main producer is ___E:Paraguay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay)___ .
Marijuana is dried and mixed with ___E:binding agents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binder_(material))___ that make it toxic and highly harmful to health.

It is cut into the shape of bricks ( ladrillos ) and sold for a low price in ___E:Argentina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina)___ , Brazil, Chile, ___E:Peru U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru)___ , ___E:Venezuela U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela)___ , and even the United States.

Cannabis is ___E:indigenous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_(ecology))___ to Central or South Asia  and its uses for fabric and rope dates back to the ___E:Neolithic age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_age)___ in China and Japan.
It is unclear when cannabis first became known for its psychoactive properties.

The oldest archeological evidence for the burning of cannabis was found in Romanian ___E:kurgans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurgan)___ dated 3,500 BC, and scholars suggest that the drug was first used in ritual ceremonies by ___E:Proto-Indo-European U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Indo-Europeans)___ tribes living in the ___E:Pontic-Caspian steppe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontic%E2%80%93Caspian_steppe)___ during the ___E:Chalcolithic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalcolithic)___ period, a custom they eventually spread throughout Western Eurasia during the ___E:Indo-European migrations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_migrations)___ .

Some research suggests that the ancient ___E:Indo-Iranian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Iranians)___ drug ___E:soma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soma_(drink))___ , mentioned in the ___E:Vedas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veda)___ , sometimes contained cannabis.
This is based on the discovery of a basin containing cannabis in a shrine of the ___E:second millennium BC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_millennium_BC)___ in Turkmenistan.
Cannabis was known to the ___E:ancient Assyrians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Assyrian_people)___ , who discovered its psychoactive properties through the Iranians.
Using it in some religious ceremonies, they called it qunubu (meaning "way to produce smoke"), a probable origin of the modern word cannabis .

The Iranians also introduced cannabis to the Scythians, ___E:Thracians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians)___ and ___E:Dacians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacia)___ , whose shamans (the kapnobatai – "those who walk on smoke/clouds") burned cannabis infructescences to induce ___E:trance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trance)___ .

The plant was used in China before 2800 BC, and found therapeutic use in India by 1000 BC, where it was used ___E:in food and drink U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_edible)___ , including bhang .
Cannabis has an ancient history of ritual use and has been used by religions around the world.

It has been used as a drug for both ___E:recreational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_marijuana)___ and ___E:entheogenic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entheogenic_use_of_cannabis)___ purposes and in various ___E:traditional medicines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_medicine)___ for centuries.

The earliest evidence of cannabis smoking has been found in the 2,500-year-old tombs of Jirzankal Cemetery in the ___E:Pamir Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamir_Mountains)___ in Western China, where cannabis residue were found in burners with charred pebbles possibly used during funeral rituals.

Hemp seeds discovered by archaeologists at ___E:Pazyryk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazyryk_burials)___ suggest early ceremonial practices like eating by the Scythians occurred during the 5th to 2nd century BC, confirming previous historical reports by Herodotus.

It was used by Muslims in various ___E:Sufi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi)___ orders as early as the ___E:Mamluk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk)___ period, for example by the ___E:Qalandars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qalandariyya)___ .
Smoking pipes uncovered in Ethiopia and carbon-dated to around c. AD 1320 were found to have traces of cannabis.

Cannabis was introduced to the ___E:New World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World)___ by the Spaniards in 1530–1545.    Following an 1836–1840 travel in North Africa and the Middle East, French physician ___E:Jacques-Joseph Moreau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Joseph_Moreau)___ wrote on the psychological effects of cannabis use; he founded the Paris' ___E:Club des Hashischins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_des_Hashischins)___ in 1844.  In 1842, Irish physician ___E:William Brooke O'Shaughnessy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Brooke_O%27Shaughnessy)___ , who had studied the drug while working as a medical officer in Bengal with the ___E:East India Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company)___ , brought a quantity of cannabis with him on his return to ___E:Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland)___ , provoking renewed interest in the West.  Examples of classic literature of the period featuring cannabis include Les paradis artificiels (1860) by ___E:Charles Baudelaire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Baudelaire)___ and The Hasheesh Eater (1857) by ___E:Fitz Hugh Ludlow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fitz_Hugh_Ludlow)___ .
Cannabis was criminalized in some countries beginning in the 14th century and was illegal in most countries by the middle of the 20th century.

The colonial government of Mauritius banned cannabis in 1840 over concerns on its effect on Indian indentured workers;  the same occurred in Singapore in 1870.  In the United States, the first restrictions on sale of cannabis came in 1906 (in the ___E:District of Columbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia)___ ).

Canada criminalized cannabis in The Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, 1923 ,  before any reports of the use of the drug in Canada, but eventually legalized its consumption for recreational and medicinal purposes in 2018.

In 1925, a compromise was made at an international conference in ___E:Geneva U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva)___ about the ___E:Second International Opium Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_International_Opium_Convention)___ that banned exportation of "Indian hemp" to countries that had prohibited its use, and requiring importing countries to issue certificates approving the importation and stating that the shipment was required "exclusively for medical or scientific purposes".
It also required parties to "exercise an effective control of such a nature as to prevent the illicit international traffic in Indian hemp and especially in the resin".
In the United States in 1937, the ___E:Marihuana Tax Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marihuana_Tax_Act_of_1937)___ was passed,  and prohibited the production of hemp in addition to cannabis.
In 1972, the Dutch government divided drugs into more- and less-dangerous categories, with cannabis being in the lesser category.
Accordingly, possession of 30 grams (1.1 oz) or less was made a misdemeanor.

Cannabis has been available for recreational use in ___E:coffee shops U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffeeshop_(Netherlands))___ since 1976.  Cannabis products are only sold openly in certain local "coffeeshops" and possession of up to 5 grams (0.18 oz) for personal use is decriminalized, however: the police may still confiscate it, which often happens in car checks near the border.

Other types of sales and transportation are not permitted, although the general approach toward cannabis was lenient even before official ___E:decriminalization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decriminalization)___ .

In Uruguay, President ___E:Jose Mujica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Mujica)___ signed legislation to ___E:legalize recreational cannabis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Uruguay)___ in December 2013, making Uruguay the first country in the modern era to legalize cannabis.

In August 2014, Uruguay legalized growing up to six plants at home, as well as the formation of growing clubs ( ___E:Cannabis social club U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_social_club)___ ), and a state-controlled ___E:marijuana dispensary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marijuana_dispensary)___ regime.

As of 17 October 2018 [update] , when recreational use of cannabis was legalized in Canada, ___E:dietary supplements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_supplement)___ for human use and ___E:veterinary health products U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holistic_veterinary_medicine)___ containing not more than 10 parts per million of THC extract were approved for marketing; ___E:Nabiximols U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabiximols)___ (as Sativex) is used as a prescription drug in Canada.

The United Nations' World Drug Report stated that cannabis "was the world's most widely produced, trafficked, and consumed drug in the world in 2010", and estimated between 128 million and 238 million users globally in 2015.

Cannabis has been one of the most used ___E:psychoactive drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoactive_drug)___ in the world since the late 20th century, following only ___E:tobacco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco)___ and ___E:alcohol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(drug))___ in popularity.

According to Vera Rubin, the use of cannabis has been encompassed by two major cultural complexes over time: a continuous, traditional ___E:folk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_culture)___ stream, and a more circumscribed, contemporary configuration.

The former involves both sacred and secular use, and is usually based on small-scale cultivation: the use of the plant for ___E:cordage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rope)___ , clothing, medicine, food, and a "general use as an ___E:euphoriant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoriant)___ and symbol of fellowship."   The second stream of expansion of cannabis use encompasses "the use of hemp for commercial manufacturers utilizing large-scale cultivation primarily as a fiber for mercantile purposes"; but it is also linked to the search for ___E:psychedelic experiences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_experience)___ (which can be traced back to the formation of the Parisian ___E:Club des Hashischins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_des_Hashischins)___ ).
Since the beginning of the 20th century, most countries have enacted ___E:laws U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_(drugs))___ against the cultivation, possession or transfer of cannabis.
These laws have had an adverse effect on cannabis cultivation for non-recreational purposes, but there are many regions where handling of cannabis is legal or licensed.

Many jurisdictions have lessened the penalties for possession of small quantities of cannabis so that it is punished by confiscation and sometimes a fine, rather than imprisonment, focusing more on those who traffic the drug on the ___E:black market U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_market)___ .

In some areas where cannabis use had been historically tolerated, new restrictions were instituted, such as the closing of cannabis coffee shops near the borders of the Netherlands,  and closing of coffee shops near secondary schools in the Netherlands.

In ___E:Copenhagen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen)___ , Denmark in 2014, mayor ___E:Frank Jensen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Jensen)___ discussed possibilities for the city to legalize cannabis production and commerce.
Some jurisdictions use free voluntary or mandatory treatment programs for frequent known users.
Simple possession can carry long prison terms in some countries, particularly in East Asia, where the sale of cannabis may lead to a sentence of life in prison or even execution.

Political parties, non-profit organizations, and causes based on the legalization of medical cannabis or legalizing the plant entirely (with some restrictions) have emerged in such countries as China and Thailand.

In December 2012, the U.S. state of ___E:Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state))___ became the first state to officially legalize cannabis in a state law ( ___E:Washington Initiative 502 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Initiative_502)___ ) (but still illegal by ___E:federal law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_the_United_States)___ ),  with the state of ___E:Colorado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado)___ following close behind ( ___E:Colorado Amendment 64 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Amendment_64)___ ).

On 1 January 2013, the first cannabis " ___E:club U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_Social_Club)___ " for private marijuana smoking (no buying or selling, however) was allowed for the first time in Colorado.
The California Supreme Court decided in May 2013 that local governments can ban medical cannabis dispensaries despite a state law in California that permits the use of cannabis for medical purposes.
At least 180 cities across California have enacted bans in recent years.

On 30 April 2024, the United States ___E:Department of Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Department_of_Justice)___ announced it would move to reclassify cannabis from a Schedule I to a ___E:Schedule III controlled substance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled_Substances_Act#Schedule_III)___ .
In December 2013, ___E:Uruguay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay)___ became the first country to legalize growing, sale and use of cannabis.
After a long delay in implementing the retail component of the law, in 2017 sixteen pharmacies were authorized to sell cannabis commercially.
On 19 June 2018, the Canadian Senate passed a bill and the Prime Minister announced the effective legalization date as 17 October 2018.   Canada is the second country to legalize the drug.
In November 2015, ___E:Uttarakhand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttarakhand)___ became the first state of India to legalize the cultivation of hemp for industrial purposes.

Usage within the Hindu and Buddhist cultures of the ___E:Indian subcontinent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent)___ is common, with many street vendors in India openly selling products infused with cannabis, and traditional medical practitioners in Sri Lanka selling products infused with cannabis for recreational purposes and well as for religious celebrations.
Indian laws criminalizing cannabis date back to the ___E:colonial period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_India)___ .
India and Sri Lanka have allowed cannabis to be taken in the context of traditional culture for recreational/celebratory purposes and also for medicinal purposes.

On 17 October 2015, Australian health minister ___E:Sussan Ley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussan_Ley)___ presented a new law that will allow the ___E:cultivation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture)___ of cannabis for scientific research and medical trials on patients.

On 17 October 2018, ___E:Canada legalized cannabis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Canada)___ for recreational adult use  making it the second country in the world to do so after Uruguay and the first G7 nation.

This legalization comes with regulation similar to that of ___E:alcohol in Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_drinks_in_Canada)___ , age restrictions, limiting home production, distribution, consumption areas and sale times.

Laws around use vary from province to province including age limits, retail structure, and growing at home.  The ___E:Canadian Licensed Producer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_licensed_producers_of_medical_marijuana_in_Canada)___ system aims to become the Gold Standard in the world for safe and secure cannabis production,  including provisions for a robust craft cannabis industry where many expect opportunities for experimenting with different strains.

As the drug has increasingly been seen as a health issue instead of criminal behavior, cannabis has also been legalized or ___E:decriminalized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decriminalization)___ in: ___E:Czech Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic)___ ,  ___E:Colombia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia)___ ,   ___E:Ecuador U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador)___ ,    ___E:Portugal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal)___ ,  ___E:South Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_South_Africa)___  and Canada.
Medical marijuana was legalized in Mexico in mid-2017 and legalized for recreational use in June 2021.
Germany legalized cannabis for recreational use in April 2024.

As of 2022, ___E:Uruguay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Uruguay)___ and ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Canada)___ are the only countries that have fully legalized the cultivation, consumption and bartering of recreational cannabis nationwide.   ___E:In the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_cannabis_by_U.S._jurisdiction)___ , 24 states, 3 territories, and the District of Columbia have legalized the recreational use of cannabis – though the drug remains illegal at the federal level.

Laws vary from state to state when it comes to the commercial sale. Court rulings in ___E:Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country))___ and South Africa have led to the legalization of cannabis consumption, but not legal sales.

A policy of limited enforcement has also been adopted in many countries, in particular Spain and the ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands)___ where the sale of cannabis is tolerated at licensed establishments.
Contrary to popular belief, cannabis is not legal in the Netherlands,  but it has been decriminalized since the 1970s.

In 2021, ___E:Malta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malta)___ was the first ___E:European Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union)___ member to legalize the use of cannabis for recreational purposes.

In ___E:Estonia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia)___ , it is only legal to sell cannabis products with a THC content of less than 0.2%, although products may contain more cannabidiol.  ___E:Lebanon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon)___ has recently become the first Arab country to legalize the plantation of cannabis for medical use.
Penalties for illegal recreational use ranges from confiscation or small fines to jail time and even death.
In some countries, citizens can be punished if they have used the drug in another country, including Singapore and South Korea.

Sinsemilla (Spanish for "without seed") is the dried, seedless (i.e. ___E:parthenocarpic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenocarpy)___ ) ___E:infructescences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infructescence)___ of female ___E:cannabis plants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_sativa)___ .

Because THC production drops off once pollination occurs, the male plants (which produce little THC themselves) are eliminated before they shed pollen to prevent pollination, thus inducing the development of ___E:parthenocarpic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenocarpy)___ fruits gathered in dense ___E:infructescences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infructescence)___ .

Advanced cultivation techniques such as ___E:hydroponics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_(drug)_cultivation#Hydroponic_cultivation)___ , ___E:cloning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_(drug)_cultivation#Feminized_seeds)___ , ___E:high-intensity artificial lighting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_(drug)_cultivation#Light)___ , and ___E:the sea of green method U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_(drug)_cultivation#SOG)___ are frequently employed as a response (in part) to prohibition enforcement efforts that make outdoor cultivation more risky.
"Skunk" refers to several named strains of potent cannabis, grown through selective breeding and sometimes ___E:hydroponics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroponics)___ .
It is a cross-breed of Cannabis sativa and C. indica (although other strains of this mix exist in abundance).
Skunk cannabis potency ranges usually from 6% to 15% and rarely as high as 20%.
The average THC level in coffee shops in the Netherlands is about 18–19%.

The average levels of THC in cannabis sold in the United States rose dramatically between the 1970s and 2000.  This is disputed for various reasons, and there is little consensus as to whether this is a fact or an artifact of poor testing methodologies.

According to Daniel Forbes writing for slate.com, the relative strength of modern strains are likely skewed because undue weight is given to much more expensive and potent, but less prevalent, samples.
Some suggest that results are skewed by older testing methods that included low-THC-content plant material such as leaves in the samples, which are excluded in contemporary tests.
Others believe that modern strains actually are significantly more potent than older ones.

The main producing countries of cannabis are Afghanistan,  Canada,  China, Colombia,  India,  Jamaica,  Lebanon,  Mexico,  Morocco,  the Netherlands, Pakistan, Paraguay,  Spain,  Thailand, Turkey, the United Kingdom,  and the United States.
The price or street value of cannabis varies widely depending on geographic area and potency.
Prices and overall markets have also varied considerably over time.

After some U.S. states legalized cannabis, street prices began to drop. In Colorado, the price of smokable buds (infructescences) dropped 40 percent between 2014 and 2019, from $200 per ounce to $120 per ounce ($7 per gram to $4.19 per gram).

The ___E:European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Monitoring_Centre_for_Drugs_and_Drug_Addiction)___ reports that typical retail prices in Europe for cannabis varied from €2 to €20 per gram in 2008, with a majority of European countries reporting prices in the range €4–10.
The gateway hypothesis states that cannabis use increases the probability of trying "harder" drugs.

The hypothesis has been hotly debated as it is regarded by some as the primary rationale for the United States prohibition on cannabis use.   A ___E:Pew Research Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center)___ poll found that political opposition to marijuana use was significantly associated with concerns about the health effects and whether legalization would increase cannabis use by children.
Some studies state that while there is no proof for the gateway hypothesis,  young cannabis users should still be considered as a risk group for intervention programs.

Other findings indicate that ___E:hard drug U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_and_soft_drugs)___ users are likely to be ___E:poly-drug users U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poly_drug_use)___ , and that interventions must address the use of multiple drugs instead of a single hard drug.  Almost two-thirds of the poly drug users in the 2009–2010 Scottish Crime and Justice Survey used cannabis.

The gateway effect may appear due to social factors involved in using any illegal drug. Because of the illegal status of cannabis, its consumers are likely to find themselves in situations allowing them to acquaint with individuals using or selling other illegal drugs.

Studies have shown that alcohol and tobacco may additionally be regarded as gateway drugs;  however, a more parsimonious explanation could be that cannabis is simply more readily available (and at an earlier age) than illegal hard drugs. [citation needed] In turn, alcohol and tobacco are typically easier to obtain at an earlier age than is cannabis (though the reverse may be true in some areas), thus leading to the "gateway sequence" in those individuals, since they are most likely to experiment with any drug offered.
A related alternative to the gateway hypothesis is the common liability to addiction (CLA) theory.
It states that some individuals are, for various reasons, willing to try multiple recreational substances.
The "gateway" drugs are merely those that are (usually) available at an earlier age than the harder drugs.
Researchers have noted in an extensive review that it is dangerous to present the sequence of events described in gateway "theory" in causative terms as this hinders both research and intervention.

In 2020, the ___E:National Institute on Drug Abuse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_on_Drug_Abuse)___ released a study backing allegations that marijuana is a gateway to harder drugs, though not for the majority of marijuana users.

The National Institute on Drug Abuse determined that marijuana use is "likely to precede use of other licit and illicit substances" and that "adults who reported marijuana use during the first wave of the survey were more likely than adults who did not use marijuana to develop an alcohol use disorder within 3 years; people who used marijuana and already had an alcohol use disorder at the outset were at greater risk of their alcohol use disorder worsening.
Marijuana use is also linked to other substance use disorders including nicotine addiction."  It also reported that "These findings are consistent with the idea of marijuana as a "gateway drug".
However, the majority of people who use marijuana do not go on to use other, "harder" substances.
Also, cross-sensitization is not unique to marijuana.
Alcohol and nicotine also prime the brain for a heightened response to other drugs and are, like marijuana, also typically used before a person progresses to other, more harmful substances."
Research on cannabis is challenging since the plant is ___E:illegal in most countries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_cannabis)___ .

Research-grade samples of the drug are difficult to obtain for research purposes, unless granted under authority of national regulatory agencies, such as the US ___E:Food and Drug Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration)___ .
There are also other difficulties in researching the effects of cannabis.
Many people who smoke cannabis also smoke tobacco.
This causes confounding factors, where questions arise as to whether the tobacco, the cannabis, or both that have caused a cancer.
Another difficulty researchers have is in recruiting people who smoke cannabis into studies.
Because cannabis is an illegal drug in many countries, people may be reluctant to take part in research, and if they do agree to take part, they may not say how much cannabis they actually smoke.
